opus-5.5.text:
I think the exploratory phase is honestly the most important and also the most uncomfortable part of research. Many people want to skip it. They want to jump straight to a well-defined problem with a benchmark and a number to beat, because that feels safe and productive. But if you do that, you usually end up doing incremental work, because the problem was already defined by someone else.

So my first suggestion is to give yourself permission to be lost for a while. In the exploratory phase you shouldn't judge yourself by output. You should judge yourself by whether your understanding is changing. Are you seeing something about the problem that you didn't see a week ago? If yes, that's progress, even if you have no paper and no clean result.

Second, I think it's very important to run small, fast experiments, almost like sketches. Don't build a huge system before you know whether the idea has any signal. Try ten cheap things, look at the results very carefully, and especially look for the surprising ones. Often the real direction is not the hypothesis you started with. It's some weird observation on the side that doesn't fit your mental model. Many good projects come from taking that anomaly seriously instead of treating it as noise.

Third, ask whether the direction is worth pursuing if it works. I often ask students: suppose everything goes perfectly, what changes? Does it change how people think about the problem, or does it just add one more row to a table? If the best case is still small, maybe it's not worth months of your life. I'd rather work on something with a big upside and some risk of failing than something guaranteed to work but doesn't matter much.

Fourth, talk to people, but don't let consensus decide for you. It's good to get feedback, but sometimes if everyone immediately agrees your idea is good, it may already be obvious, and many groups are working on it. Some of the most interesting directions initially sound a bit strange or even wrong to others. You need conviction, but conviction based on evidence you've seen yourself, not just a feeling.

And finally, know when to converge. Exploration can't be forever. At some point you need to commit, simplify the story, and push it hard. I think good researchers alternate between these two modes: divergent, open, curious, and then focused, almost stubborn execution. The skill is recognizing which mode you should be in at a given moment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the exploratory phase is the part most people try to shortcut, and that's exactly where it goes wrong.

When I start something new, I try not to begin with a method. I begin with a question that genuinely bothers me. Something like, why does this thing that everyone treats as settled actually work? Or why does something that should work, not work? If I can't articulate what's confusing me in one or two sentences, I'm probably not ready to commit a student's year to it.

Then there's a phase that doesn't look productive from the outside. You read a lot, you run small, almost embarrassingly simple experiments, and you talk to people. The goal isn't results yet. The goal is to build intuition about where the real difficulty lives. A lot of problems look hard because the field has layered complexity on top of them, and once you strip that away, the core question is much cleaner. ConvNeXt came partly from that kind of exercise. We weren't trying to beat Transformers. We wanted to understand what was actually responsible for the gap, and that question turned out to be more interesting than any single architecture.

I also tell students to pay attention to their own confusion. If a paper's explanation feels unsatisfying to you, don't assume you're missing something. Often the explanation really is incomplete, and that gap is a direction. The field moves fast, so people accept a lot of folk wisdom without checking it. Revisiting that folk wisdom carefully is underrated.

Another thing is taste for simplicity. In the exploratory stage, I'm looking for an idea that's simple enough that if it works, I'll understand why it works, and if it fails, I'll learn something. Complicated ideas can succeed for reasons you never figure out, and then you can't build on them.

And finally, I'd say don't optimize too early for whether something will be publishable. If you chase what's hot, you're competing with everyone who had the same thought three months ago. The directions I've been happiest with usually looked a little unfashionable at the start. The exploration phase is really about giving yourself permission to be slow and curious before you become fast and focused.

astra-6.text:
I think the exploratory phase is about giving yourself room to be wrong. At the beginning, you usually don’t know which question is worth spending the next six months on. So it helps to try small experiments, follow things that surprise you, and avoid committing to a big story too early.

But exploration should still have a question behind it. What are you trying to understand? What result would change your mind? Even if an experiment doesn’t improve performance, it can be useful if it exposes an assumption that you hadn’t questioned.

Then, periodically, step back. Are these experiments starting to point toward a coherent problem? Can you explain why that problem matters beyond this particular setup? That’s when I would start narrowing the scope. You want enough freedom to discover something unexpected, and enough discipline to recognize when you’ve found a direction worth pursuing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think in the exploratory phase, you have to give yourself permission to be confused for a while. You don’t necessarily know what the right question is yet, and if you demand a clean story too early, you can miss something interesting.

I would start with a question you’re genuinely curious about, then run small experiments that help you understand it. The goal isn’t just to get a better number. It’s to learn: Why did this work? Why did that fail? Is there something here that my current understanding can’t explain? A surprising result can be more useful than a successful result, because it gives you another question to ask.

At the same time, exploration needs some discipline. You can keep trying random things forever. Periodically, step back and ask whether the experiments are building toward a clearer understanding. Can you articulate what you’ve learned and what you would test next? If you can, even a direction with disappointing results may be worth pursuing. If you can’t, it may be time to rethink the question.

So I’d give yourself room to explore, but look for a question that gets sharper as you work on it. That’s a good sign you’re finding a direction.
